title: Relative speeds, timed movement and meetings
transcript: Relative speed measures how fast a gap changes. Moving towards each other closes a gap at the sum of the two speeds. For a chase in the same direction, the gap closes at the faster speed minus the slower speed.

AMC questions about meetings, chases or moving markers often become short if you draw the gap that is changing. A Rossmoyne style problem may have delayed starts or a circular route. Track when the shared motion begins and when a full lap has passed.
Two walkers are thirty-two metres apart and walk directly towards each other at three and five metres per second. How many seconds until they meet? Think about the distance closed in one second.
The walkers together close eight metres every second. Both movements shorten the gap. Divide the starting gap by that rate. They meet after four seconds.
A runner moves at four metres per second. A second runner starts from the same point five seconds later at seven metres per second. How long after the second runner starts do they meet?

During the head start the first runner covers twenty metres. That is the gap when the chase starts. The faster runner closes three metres each second, because both are moving in the same direction. The catch happens after twenty over three seconds from the second start. Only add the head start if the question measures from the first start.

A round track is three hundred metres long. Runner A starts at two metres per second. After five seconds runner B leaves the same point in the opposite direction at three metres per second. They keep running at those speeds. At what time after A starts do they meet for the second time?

At B's start, A has run ten metres. They first meet when the combined distances reach one lap, so the unused part is two hundred and ninety metres. Together they cover five metres each second. That gives fifty-eight seconds from B's start to the first meeting. The second meeting takes one more lap at the same combined rate. Add that time and the original delay.

The total elapsed time is one hundred and twenty-three seconds after A starts. At that time the two distances add to exactly six hundred metres. The first meeting required one lap of combined movement. Adding a second lap accounts for exactly one further meeting.

A same-direction chase uses the difference in speeds. Adding the speeds would model movement towards each other instead. Timing from the later start measures only the shared motion. Check whether the requested clock started earlier.

Draw arrows for the directions and label the gap. Decide whether the movements shorten the gap together or compete. For a loop, use one full circuit between matching positions. Check the final answer by reconstructing both distances.
